articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: NACZ, Lotteries Board turn to skits to champion responsible gambling
more.description: Mbulelo Mpofu, mbulelo.smpofu@gmail.com THE country’s arts watchdog, the National Arts Council of Zimbabwe (NACZ), has partnered with the Lotteries and Gaming Board to harness the power of creative storytelling in promoting responsible gambling through the Responsible Gambling Skit Challenge. The initiative, which combines entertainment with public education, is calling on Zimbabwean skit makers to use their creativity and digital platforms to communicate the importance of making informed and responsible choices when engaging in gambling activities. Under the challenge, creatives are being invited to produce a one- to two-minute skit centred on responsible gambling and share it with the public through Facebook. Participants are required to post their skits on their Facebook pages, tag NACZ and the Lotteries and Gaming Board, and use the hashtag #ResponsibleGambling2026 to officially enter the competition. The campaign comes at a time when social media and short-form video content have become powerful tools for reaching large audiences, particularly young people. By involving skit makers, the organisers are seeking to move beyond conventional awareness campaigns and deliver the responsible gambling message in an entertaining, accessible and relatable manner. The competition’s top prize is US$1 000, with the winner determined by the skit that records the highest number of views and engagement. The deadline for submissions is 31 August, giving creatives several weeks to conceptualise, produce and publish their entries. Beyond the competition and its cash incentive, the initiative places emphasis on the need for members of the public to understand that gambling should remain a form of entertainment rather than become a source of financial dependence. Responsible gambling involves setting limits on the amount of money and time spent gambling and recognising when gambling begins to interfere with an individual’s financial stability, relationships, work or general wellbeing. It also means understanding that gambling outcomes are based on chance and that there is no guaranteed strategy for winning. The NACZ and Lotteries and Gaming Board are therefore using the creative sector as an avenue to make these messages more accessible to the wider public. For skit makers, the challenge also presents an opportunity to demonstrate how comedy, drama and storytelling can be used to address social issues without losing their entertainment value. A well-crafted one- or two-minute production can portray everyday situations, consequences of irresponsible gambling and practical ways of maintaining healthy boundaries. The campaign further highlights the growing role of Zimbabwe’s creative economy in public education. With digital content creators commanding significant audiences on social media, creative campaigns can potentially reach demographics that may not engage with traditional awareness initiatives. The organisers are encouraging participants to think creatively while ensuring that their productions clearly communicate the central message of responsible gambling. The competition also provides an avenue for emerging content creators to gain visibility, with audience engagement forming part of the criteria that will determine the winning entry. The challenge is expected to attract a wide range of comedic and dramatic interpretations of responsible gambling, while placing an important public-interest message at the heart of Zimbabwe’s increasingly influential digital creative space. At its core, the campaign seeks to remind the public that gambling should be approached with caution and self-control. It is not a means of securing guaranteed income, recovering financial losses or solving financial difficulties. The partnership between NACZ and the Lotteries and Gaming Board consequently represents an intersection between regulation, public awareness and the arts, demonstrating how creative expression can be deployed to encourage responsible behaviour and spark conversations around issues affecting communities. - Follow on X @MbuleloMpofu
